title: The Stolen Horse (Español)
summary: Two men claim ownership of a magnificent Arabian horse. Birbal asks the horse itself to reveal its real master. [ES]
full_text:
A traveler named Qasim was riding his prized black stallion to the Agra cattle fair when he met a limping beggar on the road. Taking pity on the man, Qasim let him mount the horse behind him. When they reached the city gates, Qasim dismounted and said: 'Friend, we have arrived. Please get down.'

Instead of dismounting, the beggar spurred the horse forward, shouting: 'Get down yourself! This is my horse! You were merely walking beside me!'

A fierce quarrel broke out, drawing the city watch, who brought both men before Emperor Akbar. Qasim wept: 'Sire, I gave him a ride out of charity, and he robs me!'

The beggar boldly swore: 'Lies, Your Majesty! I raised this horse from a foal! Qasim tried to drag me from the saddle!'

With no witnesses, Akbar asked Birbal to resolve the case.

Birbal ordered the horse placed in the palace stables and dismissed both men until the next morning.

The following morning, Birbal led Akbar and both claimants into the courtyard outside the stables. The horse was released into the open paddock.

Birbal said to the beggar: 'Call your horse.'

The beggar whistled and shouted, but the horse merely flicked its ears and continued grazing, completely ignoring him. When the beggar stepped close, the stallion snorted angrily and backed away.

Then Birbal turned to Qasim: 'Now, call your horse.'

Qasim stepped to the fence and spoke in a soft, gentle voice: 'Come, Badal. Come, my boy.'

The stallion lifted its head instantly. It whinnied with joy, trotted across the paddock, rested its muzzle against Qasim's chest, and began nuzzling his neck affectionately!

Birbal smiled: 'An animal cannot be bribed to lie. It knows the scent and voice of the master who feeds and grooms it with love.'

Akbar ordered the beggar whipped for ingratitude and returned the stallion to Qasim, praising Birbal's natural wisdom.

quiz.question: What is the central moral lesson taught in "The Stolen Horse"?
options: Acting in haste and anger without thinking
Believing rumors and flattery without proof

By shouting loudly and blaming others
By running away from every problem
